origin_region: Jiangsu · Suzhou · Dongting Mountains on Lake Tai
processing: Pan-fired green: tiny bud-and-leaf shoots are fired, then rolled and rubbed by hand in the cooling wok so they curl into spirals and the down is raised, and finally dried gently in the same pan; a batch takes well under an hour.
harvest_season: Spring only, from roughly mid-March to Grain Rain in late April; the earliest pre-Qingming pickings of one bud and one just-opened leaf are the top grades.
appearance_dry: Tiny, tightly curled spirals covered in silvery-white down, dark green showing through the fuzz.
appearance_liquor: Pale green-gold, slightly hazy from the down in the first steep.
appearance_wet: Minute buds with one small leaf, pale and tender, sinking quickly to the bottom of the glass.
taste_profile: Fresh and fruity-floral with hints of peach and loquat over a soft, sweet, slightly fuzzy body; brisk but not bitter.

brewing.notes: Use the top-down method: fill the glass with 75–80 °C water first, then drop the leaf on the surface and watch it sink. Pouring water onto the leaf scalds the down and turns it bitter.

vintage_note: Sold only as the current year's spring harvest, graded by picking date and leaf size: pre-Qingming Dongting lots (sold as special grades 1 and 2) are tiny, downy and expensive; yu qian lots are larger-leafed and better value. Genuine Dongting Biluochun is a protected-origin tea in short supply, while 'Biluochun' from Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou and Zhejiang is picked weeks earlier, sold all year and is much cheaper. Keep it cold and sealed; drink within the year.
description:
Bi Luo Chun comes from the Dongting hills, Dongshan and Xishan, a peninsula and an island on Lake Tai near Suzhou, and it is the small, fuzzy, curly one. The bushes there grow interplanted with loquat, peach, plum and waxberry trees, and the local claim that the fruit blossom perfumes the tea becomes at least half believable once you smell a fresh batch.

It is picked absurdly small: one bud and a leaf barely unfolded, tens of thousands of shoots to a kilo. The shoots are pan-fired, then rubbed and rolled in the cooling wok by hand until they curl into tight spirals and their white down stands up, and dried in the same pan. The whole thing takes less than an hour, and the maker's hands decide whether it ends up fragrant and intact or broken and dusty.

The cup is light, fruity and floral (peach, loquat, fresh pea) with a sweet, slightly fuzzy texture and a brisk edge that should never tip into bitterness. It is a three-steep tea. The one rule that matters: pour the water first, then drop the leaf. These shoots are so tender that water poured over them cooks them on contact; dropped into 75–80 °C water they sink slowly and open without bruising.

Buying: the Dongting origin is protected and production is small, so most 'Biluochun' in shops is the same spiral style made elsewhere, usually from larger, fuzzier leaf in Sichuan, Yunnan or Guizhou, picked a month earlier. It can be pleasant, but it is a different tea. Real Dongting leaf is tiny, the down is silvery rather than snow-white, and the first picking is not before mid-March. Ask whether it is from Dongshan or Xishan and when it was picked.

The older name 'Xia Sha Ren Xiang' ('scary fragrance') and the story of the Kangxi emperor renaming it are legends worth telling at the table, not facts to print on a label.
